concepts.name: FATF: Origin, Nature and Legal Status
key_dimensions: Founded in 1989 by G7 Summit in Paris — NOT a UN body, NOT a treaty-based organization
Intergovernmental policy-making body — its recommendations are non-binding but carry de facto compliance pressure
Secretariat housed at OECD headquarters in Paris — often confused as an OECD body (it is NOT)
Distinction from other financial bodies: IMF, BIS, FSB — overlapping mandates trap

concepts.name: FATF Mandate: Evolution from Money Laundering to Broader Threats
key_dimensions: Originally focused solely on Anti-Money Laundering (AML) in 1989
Expanded in 1996 to cover drug trafficking proceeds; post-9/11 expanded to counter-terrorism financing (CFT)
2012 revision added Proliferation Financing (weapons of mass destruction) as third pillar
Current triple mandate: AML + CFT + Countering Proliferation Financing (CPF) — sequence and scope often tested

concepts.name: FATF Recommendations: Structure and Binding Nature
key_dimensions: 40 Recommendations (after 2012 revision — merged original 40+9 Special Recommendations into 40)
Cover legal, financial, and operational measures — not legally binding but treated as international standard
Special Recommendations on Terrorist Financing: originally 9, now integrated — historical evolution is a trap
Countries assessed on technical compliance AND effectiveness — dual assessment methodology since 2013

concepts.name: FATF Membership Structure: Members vs. Observers vs. FSRB
key_dimensions: 39 members (37 member jurisdictions + 2 regional organizations: EU and GCC) — exact count fluctuates, concept matters
FATF-Style Regional Bodies (FSRBs): 9 associate members including APG, ESAAMLG, MENAFATF — India is APG member
Observer status: IMF, World Bank, UN, Egmont Group among others — distinction from full membership
India's membership: Full FATF member since 2010 — not a founding member trap

concepts.name: Grey List (Increased Monitoring) — Jurisdictions Under Increased Monitoring
key_dimensions: Formally called 'Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring' — NOT officially 'Grey List' (UPSC uses both)
Placement criteria: Strategic deficiencies in AML/CFT/CPF regimes; country commits to action plan
Consequences: Increased scrutiny, higher transaction costs, reduced FDI, correspondent banking challenges
Recent examples: Pakistan (in/out multiple times), Turkey, UAE (2022), Myanmar — geopolitical implications tested

concepts.name: Black List — High-Risk Jurisdictions Subject to a Call for Action
key_dimensions: Formally: 'High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action' — colloquially Black List
Currently: North Korea and Iran (persistently) — Myanmar added in 2022
Consequences: FATF calls on members to apply counter-measures — strongest sanction FATF can apply
Distinction from Grey List: Black List = active counter-measures; Grey List = enhanced due diligence only

concepts.name: Pakistan's FATF Journey: Geopolitical and Economic Implications
key_dimensions: Pakistan placed on Grey List in June 2018; removed in October 2022 after completing 34-point action plan
Implications for India-Pakistan relations and India's strategic use of FATF forum
Economic impact on Pakistan: credit rating, FDI decline, remittance costs during grey-listing period
Demonstrates FATF as a soft-power tool — overlap with India's foreign policy dimension

concepts.name: India's FATF Mutual Evaluation: 2023-24 Assessment
key_dimensions: India underwent 4th round Mutual Evaluation in 2023; report adopted in June 2024
Rated 'Compliant' or 'Largely Compliant' on majority of 40 Recommendations — high technical compliance
Effectiveness gaps identified: prosecution rates, beneficial ownership transparency, NPO sector oversight
Placed in 'Regular Follow-up' category — most favorable outcome; not in enhanced follow-up

concepts.name: Mutual Evaluation Process: Methodology and Ratings
key_dimensions: Peer-review process: country assessed by team of experts from other FATF members
Two pillars: Technical Compliance (40 Recommendations) rated C/LC/PC/NC; Effectiveness (11 Immediate Outcomes) rated HE/SE/ME/LE
Four follow-up categories post-evaluation: Regular Follow-up, Enhanced Follow-up, Grey List, Black List
Frequency: approximately every 5-10 years per country — 4th round currently ongoing globally

concepts.name: FATF and Terrorist Financing: Key Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Recommendation 5: Criminalisation of terrorist financing (even without link to specific act)
Targeted Financial Sanctions (TFS): UN Security Council Resolution 1267 list — FATF enforces implementation
Hawala and informal value transfer systems: Recommendation 14 specifically addresses
Non-Profit Organizations (NPOs) as vulnerability: Recommendation 8 — India's challenges with NPO monitoring

concepts.name: Beneficial Ownership and Corporate Transparency
key_dimensions: Recommendations 24 & 25: Transparency of legal persons and legal arrangements
Beneficial Owner defined as natural person who ultimately owns or controls ≥25% — threshold varies by jurisdiction
India's response: Companies Act amendments, Central Registry of Beneficial Interests — implementation gaps noted
Shell companies and nominee structures as key vulnerabilities — Panama Papers, Pandora Papers context

concepts.name: FATF and Virtual Assets / Cryptocurrency Regulation
key_dimensions: 2018: FATF extended AML/CFT requirements to Virtual Assets (VA) and Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs)
Travel Rule (Recommendation 16 extended): VASPs must share originator/beneficiary information for transactions above threshold
Implications for India's cryptocurrency regulation debate — RBI vs. MeitY jurisdiction overlap
DeFi and NFTs: FATF guidance on whether they constitute VASPs — evolving regulatory frontier

concepts.name: Egmont Group and Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs)
key_dimensions: Egmont Group: network of 166 FIUs — separate from FATF but complementary; FATF Recommendation 29 mandates FIUs
India's FIU-IND: established 2004 under Finance Ministry — receives Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs)
FIU vs. Enforcement Directorate vs. CBI: distinct roles — FIU is intelligence, not investigation agency
Information sharing between FIUs: Egmont Secure Web (ESW) — operational cooperation mechanism

concepts.name: FATF Presidency and Decision-Making Structure
key_dimensions: Presidency: rotates among members, 2-year term — Singapore held presidency 2022-24 (first Asian country)
Plenary: supreme decision-making body, meets 3 times a year — decisions by consensus
Working Groups: Policy, Risks, Trends & Methods, Global Network — operational structure
FATF has no enforcement mechanism of its own — relies on reputational pressure and peer compliance

concepts.name: Asia Pacific Group on Money Laundering (APG): India's Regional Context
key_dimensions: APG: FATF-Style Regional Body covering Asia-Pacific — 41 members including India, China, Pakistan
India is a full member of APG and FATF — dual membership significance
APG conducts its own mutual evaluations aligned with FATF standards
APG Typologies Reports: regional money laundering trends relevant for Indian context — trade-based ML, hawala

concepts.name: Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) and FATF Compliance
key_dimensions: PMLA 2002 (amended multiple times) is India's primary AML legislation — enacted partly to meet FATF standards
2023 Amendment: expanded definition of 'proceeds of crime'; strengthened beneficial ownership provisions
ED's powers under PMLA — attachment, arrest, prosecution — Supreme Court upheld in Vijay Madanlal case 2022
FATF's concern: India's low ML conviction rates despite high number of cases — effectiveness gap

concepts.name: Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML): FATF's Focus Area
key_dimensions: TBML: using international trade transactions to disguise proceeds — over/under invoicing, multiple invoicing
Particularly relevant for India: large informal trade, gold smuggling, diamond trade vulnerabilities
FATF Best Practices Paper on TBML — customs and financial intelligence coordination requirement
Distinction from hawala: TBML uses formal trade channels; hawala uses informal money transfer — often confused

concepts.name: FATF and Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs)
key_dimensions: Recommendation 12: Enhanced Due Diligence for PEPs — foreign PEPs mandatory; domestic PEPs risk-based
PEP definition: senior political officials, their family members, close associates — specific scope often tested
India's challenge: large democracy with many PEPs; banking sector compliance gaps identified
Domestic vs. Foreign PEP asymmetry: FATF allows risk-based approach for domestic PEPs — common exam trap

concepts.name: FATF Risk-Based Approach (RBA): Core Regulatory Philosophy
key_dimensions: RBA: countries and institutions should focus resources on highest ML/TF risks — not uniform rule application
National Risk Assessment (NRA): FATF requires each country to conduct and update NRA periodically
India's NRA: published 2019, updated assessments ongoing — identified real estate, gold, cryptocurrency as high-risk sectors
RBA vs. Rules-Based Approach: FATF moved from prescriptive rules to outcomes-based RBA in 2012 revision — conceptual shift

concepts.name: De-Risking and Financial Exclusion: Unintended Consequences of FATF Standards
key_dimensions: De-risking: banks terminating relationships with high-risk customers/jurisdictions to avoid compliance costs
Correspondent banking withdrawal: affects small island states, developing nations — financial exclusion risk
FATF's acknowledgment: RBA should not lead to blanket de-risking — guidance papers issued
India's relevance: remittance corridors, hawala alternatives, Jan Dhan — financial inclusion vs. AML tension
